# Decode separator-intersection lattices

Use when a large ARC grid has regular horizontal/vertical separator lines with mostly uniform background along the lines, while small colored values appear at crossings. The output may be a compressed matrix over adjacent lattice faces.

## Verified evidence from task-47246f29

Three supplied demonstrations decode exactly by reading colored values at successive separator intersections. For each output cell, inspect the four corner crossing values from a 2x2 block of adjacent intersections: if all four crossing values are the same, output that color; otherwise output the interior panel/background color (3 in the demonstrated examples).

Demo 3 gives a clear cell-by-cell check. Lattice crossing rows are 8,13,18,23,28 and columns 4,9,14,19,24,29. Output is the 4x5 matrix for adjacent pairs of crossing rows/columns. E.g. the top-left 2x2 crossing block is all 0, so output 0; the next is all 0; mixed corners map to panel background 3; the bottom-right all-4 block maps to 4. This reproduces all 20 output cells. Demo 1 similarly produces a 4x6 matrix; demo 2's all-uniform lattice decodes to a single 8.

## Region selection resolved on task-47246f29

Do not assume a universal marker-only crop rule. Form faces between consecutive separator-crossing rows and columns, but use demos to determine the lattice span and whether edge crossings are included. Mixed corner colors map to the panel/interior background; unanimous four corners map to that shared color.

Fresh demo/test sequence validates full edge-inclusive lattice extent. Demo grid 27x23 had horizontal separator rows 1,4,7,10,13,16,19,22,25 and vertical separator columns 1,8,15,22. Crop crossings to rows 4..22 and cols 1..22, yielding 6x3 faces, with mixed cells becoming background 8. Test grid 24x28 had separator rows 0,5,10,15,20 and columns 0,6,12,18,24. The edge-inclusive lattice produced 4x4 faces, mixed cells background 2, and unanimous corners copied. Accepted output:
`[[2,2,2,7],[6,2,2,2],[2,2,2,2],[2,1,2,8]]`.

Older examples for this task showed other marker-based cropping; treat crop boundaries as instance-dependent and infer them from geometry plus demos, rather than assuming standout marker colors alone define the span.

## Additional confirmed cropped-lattice variant (task-47246f29)

A fresh instance supplied two demos and a 24x28 test. The accepted output is the 5x6 matrix
`[[1,1,1,4,1,3],[5,1,4,1,1,1],[5,1,1,1,8,1],[1,1,1,1,8,8],[4,1,7,1,8,1]]`.

For this test, use horizontal colored-crossing rows 7,10,13,16,19,22 and vertical colored-crossing columns 3,7,11,15,19,23,27 (0-indexed). The selected crossing lattice is therefore 6x7, producing 5x6 faces. For each output cell, inspect the four crossing colors at the corners of that face: if all four are identical, copy that color; otherwise use the interior/panel color 1. This reproduces every accepted output cell, including unanimous 4,3,5,8,7 regions and mixed-corner cells→1. The crop is not the full visible grid: omit earlier blank separator rows and begin at the first horizontal row with colored lattice-crossings (row 7); the crossing columns begin at 3 and include the rightmost crossing at 27.

Demo 2 (26x29) independently confirms the rule and mixed-cell color. Its crossing rows were 1,9,17,25 and columns 3,9,15,21,27; four-corner unanimity/mixed→interior 7 gives the demonstrated 3x4 output `[[1,1,7,5],[7,7,7,7],[2,2,7,0]]`. The test output was finally accepted after three wrong submissions. Those failed attempts incorrectly included the unused upper lattice rows and/or extra crossing columns, and manually mis-copied several corner-consensus cells; the accepted output used precisely the 5x6 crop above. Thus dimensions/crop are as important as the consensus rule.

A separate first demo (23x29) has output 5x4 and appears broadly consistent with adjacent-crossing consensus, but at least one adjacent face with four 0 corners appears as 9 in the provided output. Do not force that demo into an unqualified rule; re-audit crossing coordinates, crop, and any selection condition cell-by-cell. This task family has known variable crops/variants. On recurrence, derive selected crossing rows/columns from the actual demos, compute each four-corner block explicitly, verify every output cell and dimensions, and do not guess a full visible lattice.

## Further verified variant evidence (task-47246f29)

A fresh stream instance (30x26) had background interior color 1, separator/background color 3, and a 9-valued lattice at separator crossings. The rows with horizontal separator bands were 4,12,20,28; the vertical lattice crossing columns were 1,8,15,22. The bottom horizontal band at row 28 had no 9-valued vertices, and the rightmost crossing column at 22 only appears in the upper lattice rows. Five demos in the same task family showed multiple varying output shapes (4x5, 2x4, 4x2, 5x3, 5x3), so output crop is not universally the full face lattice.

Two submissions of plausible full-lattice consensus-derived 3x3 outputs were wrong. The accepted output for this test was exactly 2x3:
`[[9,9,9],[1,9,1]]`.

Implications: do not infer a full rectangular output merely from all adjacent separator intervals. Demonstrations must establish which lattice rows/columns/regions are retained, and test variants may use a truncated or selected crop. Mixed cells in demos often map to the panel interior color, but never assume that the final output dimensions cover the entire visible separator lattice. Respect both the marker/lattice inclusion boundaries and edge omissions; when no precise crop is established, request a targeted demo instead of trying a likely-looking full output.

## Additional verified instance evidence (same task family)

A 21x29 demo had a 5-valued marker at the first four consecutive horizontal/vertical separator crossings along the top and lower boundary; these selected crossings defined a 1x3 output of all 5s. The remaining separators/crossings outside that selected span were not included. In a corresponding 30x30 test, the only selected crossings were color 4 at rows 0 and 27 and columns 4 and 24, yielding one face and the accepted output `[[4]]`. Thus when a sparse set of same-valued corner markers delimits a crop, form faces between consecutive selected crossing rows/columns; do not extend the output across the unmarked intervening separator lattice. Four matching corner values for the selected face yield that value.

## Further confirmed sparse-boundary crop variant (task-47246f29)

A fresh instance test was 14x28 with panel color 8 and separator color 5. Colored crossing markers occurred on horizontal separator rows 0, 4, and 8 at vertical crossing columns 0, 8, 16, and 24; row 12 was a separator but had no colored crossing markers. The accepted output was 2x3:
`[[1,8,4],[8,8,4]]`.

Use only the consecutive marker-bearing crossing rows/columns as the selected lattice; do not include a following blank separator row. For each adjacent selected crossing rectangle, output the shared color when all four corners agree, otherwise panel color 8. This yields first row `[1,8,4]` and second row `[8,8,4]`. A first attempt incorrectly included the unmarked row-12 boundary and predicted a 3x3 result; accepted dimensions confirm that unmarked outer separators do not extend the crop in this variant.

## Method

1. Locate repeating full separator rows/columns and list their intersection coordinates.
2. Derive candidate output dimensions from adjacent intersections/faces, but test whether boundary rows/columns are clipped or only a subset is selected.
3. For each candidate face, read its four crossing colors. Compare uniform corners versus mixed corners; mixed faces may map to the panel background.
4. Replay the entire candidate output against every demo, including dimensions, before applying it.
5. If a test disagrees despite exact demo replay, treat it as evidence of an unmodeled selection or clipping rule; do not repeat near-identical outputs. Strict action interface: one JSON action only.

---

# ARC grid rule inference under action constraints

Use this class-level workflow for ARC/Continual-ARC puzzles with demonstrations and a limited number of submissions or demo requests.

## Confirmed 2×2 rotated tiling variant: task-518fa031
The input expands to a 2H×2W grid of four copies of its complete pattern, rotated as follows: top-left unchanged; top-right 90° clockwise; bottom-left 90° counterclockwise; bottom-right 180°. Confirmed by a 12×12→24×24 demo (all four quadrants exactly match) and accepted 6×6→12×12, 14×14→28×28 tests; a 4×4→8×8 demo and 1×1 `[[7]]`→2×2 all-7 test are consistent. Preserve every cell and color; concatenate the left/right quadrants rowwise, then stack top/bottom halves. Build rotations explicitly and validate total dimensions and quadrant orientation. The recorded evidence uses square inputs; for a non-square recurrence, infer placement/orientation from a demo rather than assuming the same quadrant layout.

## Confirmed panel-template replication variant: task-8e04f0ad
Full-width/full-height separator lines of color 9 partition the grid into equal rectangular panels. One panel contains a pattern and the other panels are blank/background; copy the source panel's pattern into every panel at the same local coordinates, preserving separator lines. Infer panel height/width from separator spacing and identify the uniquely populated source region; do not copy separator cells as part of the pattern. Demo: 6x26 with vertical color-4 separators at columns 8 and 17; the 6x8 pattern in the first panel repeated at local coordinates in the next two panels, while separator columns remained 4. Accepted test: 20x19 with color-9 separator rows 6 and 13 and column 9, dividing into 3x2 panels of 6x9 interior cells; the populated bottom-left 6x9 tile was copied into all six panels at matching local coordinates, leaving row/column separator lines unchanged. Preserve all copied colors, including 0, and preserve background cells within the source tile.

## Infer and verify
1. Parse dimensions, colors, candidate background/edge colors, markers, and action caps. Index cells consistently by row and column.
2. Compare each demo input/output at identical coordinates. Enumerate changed cells, their original and output colors, and unchanged structures. Separate marker recoloring from rays/fills and from wholesale stripe changes.
3. Maintain a small set of plausible rules. Consider orientation, anchor, extent, endpoint exclusion, target colors, and object interaction separately; do not infer from a single visual resemblance.
4. Replay every candidate on every demo cell-by-cell. Reject any rule that misses a changed cell or alters a preserved cell. A transformation is not validated merely because one part fits.
5. Apply the surviving rule to the test input, preserve unrelated cells, and validate dimensions, row lengths, bounds, and palette before submission.

## Demo/action budget
- A request costs score. Request only when a concrete ambiguity remains and explain internally which candidate rules the next example should distinguish.
- Use only actions authorized by the puzzle interface. In a submit/request_demos/finish protocol, do not call unrelated tools or task-planning actions; reason from visible grids and output only the required JSON action.
- After incorrect feedback, do not submit a near-identical grid with superficial edits. Treat the candidate rule as suspect, identify which assumptions were unproven, and reconstruct the output from the demos.
- If demos leave a behavior unresolved, do not present it as established. Seek a discriminating example only if worth its cost; otherwise make the most evidence-supported choice within the remaining attempt budget.

## Directional lines and boundary rays
For markers near edge bars, verify independently: ray direction, whether the marker becomes the ray color or a special color, where the ray stops, whether the boundary is preserved, and whether only marker-containing rows/columns activate. For diagonal rays, check each next cell: a current task-9bc5df6e run had rays extend through background to the boundary, but a test ray's next cell was a foreign non-background color and the accepted output preserved that blocker and added no ray. Thus use background-only extension when supported and never overwrite foreign-color cells without demo evidence. Other task-9bc5df6e recurrences had rays reaching boundaries; treat variant scope carefully. Do not assume opposite-edge symmetry. Special complete bands or stripes may have a separate selection rule; preserve them unless demonstrations establish how they are selected. See `references/boundary-ray-case.md` for a documented example and its limitations.

### Additional accepted blocker-sensitive no-op recurrence (7x24 test)
Three demos and the accepted test establish: extend selected same-color diagonal pairs outward through background, stopping at grid edges or non-background blockers. Demo 1 (9x23, bg1): 5 pair at (4,13),(5,14) extends NW from (4,13) through (3,12),(2,11),(1,10),(0,9); 7 pair at (6,14),(7,13) extends SW from (7,13) to (8,12). Demo 2 (11x23, bg9): 0 pair at (4,2),(5,1) extends up-right from (4,2) through (3,3),(2,4),(1,5),(0,6); 5 pair at (7,2),(8,3) extends down-right from (7,2) through (9,4),(10,5), preserving existing cells. Demo 3 (11x8, bg7) has a tiny adjacent 4/9 and 0 motif with no same-color diagonal pair and is unchanged. Accepted test (7x24, bg2) is exactly unchanged: 7s at (0,5),(1,4) suggest a diagonal, but one direction is out of bounds and the other immediately encounters foreign color 1 at (2,3); preserve blocker and do not continue through it. The 7 at (2,4) is vertical-adjacent, not a diagonal continuation. When all plausible rays are out of bounds or blocked, preserve the entire grid. Note an early guessed ray submission was wrong; unchanged output was accepted after valid-grid submission.

### Additional diagonal-ray run task-9bc5df6e (accepted test; selector nuanced)
A further run had three demos and an accepted 25x6 test. Background-only diagonal rays are supported, but direction and activation must be inferred per motif; do not extend every diagonal pair in both directions.

- Demo 1 (28x20, background 6): preserve the multicolor seed near rows 0–2, cols 7–10. Extend color 7 from (0-indexed row 2,col 7) diagonally down-left through background to (row 9,col 0), and color 4 from (row 2,col 10) diagonally down-right through background to (row 11,col 19). Other cells unchanged.
- Demo 2 (13x15, background 9): preserve seed motif around rows 7–9, cols 11–13. Extend color 6 down-left from (row 9,col 11), adding (10,10),(11,9),(12,8). Other cells unchanged.
- Demo 3 (28x9, background 3): preserve seed at rows 24–26, cols 0–2; extend color 9 up-right from (row 24,col 2), adding (23,3),(22,4),(21,5),(20,6),(19,7),(18,8). Other cells unchanged.
- Accepted test (25x6, background 3): add only color 4 at (0-indexed row 20,col 5), continuing the diagonal from existing color-4 cells (row 21,col 4) and (row 22,col 3). All other cells, including the nearby diagonal color-9 pair, remained unchanged. Several guesses extending color 9 in one or both directions, or extending both colors, were wrong. A diagonal seed alone is insufficient to activate a ray; preserve non-selected/blocked motifs and infer selection from full local motif geometry/context. This run confirms one ray can be selected while a nearby-looking diagonal pair is untouched. Do not infer a broader selector beyond these demos. See also the variant history below.

## Confirmed task-a8c517ee variant: fill enclosed frame interiors by parity
Two demos and an accepted test establish that outlined rectangular/square frames retain their borders while enclosed background cells are filled. The demonstrated outputs show fill color 2 when both interior dimensions are even (demo 2: a 2x2 hole; accepted test: a 6x6 hole), and color 7 when at least one interior dimension is odd (demo 1: 5x5; demo 2: 5x5, 5x7, 1x1, and 3x3; accepted test: 3x3 and 1x1). Another accepted 25x16 test had a 4-frame with a 4x4 interior (filled 2) and a 4-frame with a 5x5 interior (filled 7), confirming same-color frames can receive different fills based on their interior dimensions. Other grid cells and frame borders stay unchanged. This parity mapping fits all observed cases. A further accepted 21x18 recurrence confirmed it: a color-4 frame with a 2x2 interior was filled with 2, while color-1 frame with 5x5 interior and color-8 frame with 1x1 interior were filled with 7; all frame borders and unrelated cells were preserved. Do not fill frame borders or globally recolor frame colors. Accepted test 15x20: the 4-frame at rows 0–7, cols 8–15 has 6x6 interior filled 2; the 5-frame at rows 9–13, cols 10–14 has 3x3 interior filled 7; the 6-frame at rows 10–12, cols 3–5 has its single interior cell filled 7. First submission incorrectly used 7 for the even 6x6 hole; accepted output confirms the parity mapping. A further accepted 23x22 recurrence has differently colored frames (colors 1, 4, 6, 8, 9) with 1x1, 2x2, 3x3, 3x2, 4x4 interiors. Fill 2x2 and 4x4 interiors with 2 because both dimensions are even; fill the others with 7 because at least one dimension is odd. The small 3x3 outer frames with 1x1 holes also receive 7. All borders, background (3), and unrelated content remain unchanged. This additionally confirms the rule is independent of frame color and applies to rectangular holes.

## Confirmed full monochromatic line recoloring variant: task-07cb84d7
A demo and accepted test establish that identify every row and column whose cells are all the same color, then recolor those complete lines to color 2. Keep all cells outside those qualifying lines unchanged; intersections are also 2. The line color need not match between lines. In the demo (21x28), complete color-1 rows (indices 1, 4, 14) and columns (indices 0, 5) became color 2; all partial/singleton color-1 cells and color-3 cells remained as-is. In the accepted 12x8 test, complete color-5 columns 2 and 3 and complete color-5 row 9 became color 2, while other 5s and all 7s stayed unchanged. Check full-line status against the original input, not incrementally modified cells. A further accepted 15x7 recurrence confirms the rule: the all-8 rows 2 and 14 and all-8 column 0 became 2; all other cells remained unchanged, including partial 8s. A further task-07cb84d7 recurrence with background 5 and line color 9 confirmed that every fully monochromatic row or column is recolored to 2, including all qualifying lines regardless of whether there is only one or several; in that 26x23 test, full rows 9 and 25 and full columns 9, 15, 18, and 22 were the qualifying lines. Validate by enumerating every row and column against the original input before generating output—missing even one full line causes a wrong answer. The rule is line-color agnostic: demonstrations also use monochromatic lines of colors 0, 3, and 5, all recolored to 2. Preserve every cell outside qualifying lines.

## Additional confirmed task-fce33c1b run: horizontal periodic stripe completion
A separate recurrence was accepted with sparse/incorrect horizontal stripe colors completed to a repeating row-color sequence. Infer the stripe orientation and period from the instance demos; task ID and prior diagonal cases do not fix either. Demos in this run: (1) 7x7 input had full rows `[0,7,6,6,3,2,4]`; output `[4,7,6,6,3,2,4]`, consistent with period 6 and sequence `[4,7,6,6,3,2]` (row 0 is its matching residue, replacing an anomalous 0). (2) Sparse down-right diagonal 9s produced a uniform 9 grid; treat this as an observed demo, not evidence to fill unknown residues as 9 in a different instance. (3) 21x21 sparse horizontal rows 2,8,4,0,0,0,2,0,...,7,...,4,...,4,2 became the repeated period-8 sequence `[2,8,4,4,2,7,2,4]`. Accepted 4x4 test had rows `[0,4,4,6]` and output `[6,4,4,6]`, consistent with period 3 sequence `[6,4,4]`. Preserve the row-pattern phase and fill/correct each full stripe according to the demo-derived repeat. Determine the smallest period that is valid against every clue and replay demos; do not assume a period from task ID, and do not transfer the separate diagonal-residue rule's uncertain missing-class guesses.

## Additional confirmed task-fce33c1b recurrence: horizontal periodic row-color bands (accepted)
This distinct run used full-width monochrome horizontal stripes separated by blank rows; fill every row with the color of its vertical residue class, producing a horizontally uniform output. Infer the smallest period compatible with all colored-row clues and use the clue colors to determine each residue; the period and palette can vary, and task-fce33c1b also has a diagonal-residue variant, so choose orientation from the current demos. In this accepted test, 28x28 input had known rows (0-indexed) r0=4, r7=9, r8=6, r11=1, r21=6, r22=3. The output repeats period 6 with row sequence `[4,9,6,6,3,1]`, each value across the entire row; this exactly matches all six clues and was accepted. Thus rows 0–27 follow that six-value sequence cyclically. Current demos included a separate diagonal-residue periodic-grid pair, plus horizontal examples: a 4x4 case with row sequence 9,4 alternating after filling blank rows, and a 16x16 case whose completed horizontal row colors repeat `[7,6,5,5,3,8]` every six rows. Another 9x9 horizontal demo filled blank top rows while preserving the shown row bands. Treat the distinct diagonal demo as evidence only for its own orientation variant. Validate all explicit stripe clues against candidate period and residues before submitting; do not assume that a repeating row sequence implies a diagonal pattern.

Further solved recurrence of task-fce33c1b confirms period is instance-specific, not fixed by task ID or other demos. Demo: 14x14 input had full rows at indices 1:8, 5:2, 8:5, 9:2, 10:2, 12:2, with blanks elsewhere. Output repeats the six-row sequence `[2,8,5,2,2,2]` (e.g. output rows 0–13 are `[2,8,5,2,2,2,2,8,5,2,2,2,2,8]`). On this run's 28x28 test, the known rows were r0=5, r4=3, r20=7; the accepted output repeated period-3 sequence `[5,3,7]` across rows, i.e. each row was horizontally uniform and row color was `[5,3,7][r mod 3]`. This explicitly demonstrates that the demo's period 6 must not be copied to the test; infer the test period from its own stripe clues and validate all clues. Preserve the horizontal-row orientation and emit a full uniformly colored grid.

## Confirmed diagonal-residue periodic fill variant: task-fce33c1b
Sparse colored straight lines encode a periodic full-grid pattern. Infer the invariant coordinate (`r+c` for up-right diagonals, `c-r` for down-right diagonals, `r` for horizontal stripes), then map each residue class to its observed color and fill the complete grid. Demo sequences and periods are instance-specific; task IDs recur with variants. Do not infer missing residue colors from other demos or arbitrarily fill them with background. Crucial period rule learned from an 8-demo run that ended unsuccessfully: the period is the smallest **valid** repeat compatible with all marked lines, where same residues must have identical colors, but not necessarily simply the minimum visual gap. Explicitly enumerate candidate periods and check every clue before submitting. In that run, test line sums/colors were 9→1, 28→5, 36→3, 50→3, 52→4. A period-5 interpretation had residues `{0:3,1:3,2:4,3:5,4:1}`; period 7 `{0:5,1:3,2:1,3:4}`; period 14 `{0:5,8:3,9:1,10:4}`; period 13 `{0:4,2:5,9:1,10:3,11:3}`; period 10 `{0:3,2:4,6:3,8:5,9:1}`. Multiple fits remained, so the demonstrations did not identify the test's missing residue classes. Eight successive guesses were rejected, including zero-filling unknown residues and intuitive p7 palettes. Treat this as an unresolved variant: do not claim an accepted rule for it; audit actual demos for any clues about how period is encoded, test candidate mappings against all marked stripes, and avoid speculative submissions when multiple periods/sequences remain consistent.

Other validated cases: Demo 2 (23x23) used horizontal rows with period 2, row residue 0→2 and residue 1→1. A 27x27 horizontal demo had period 6, residue colors `[4,8,3,6,6,5]`; sparse stripes at rows 6(4), 7(8), 9(6), 14(3), 22(6), 23(5) establish the repeat, including adjacent equal colors. An accepted 22x22 horizontal test had period 6 and residue colors `[6,4,9,9,7,2]`, with input rows 2(9), 12(2), 15(4), 17(9), 18(7), 20–21(6). An accepted 12x12 down-right diagonal test had invariant `c-r`, period 4, residues `[7,6,8,2]`, yielding rows `[7,6,8,2]`, `[2,7,6,8]`, `[8,2,7,6]`, `[6,8,2,7]` repeating. Output is a full periodic pattern, not preservation of sparse input.

## Additional task-ebb0e4e4 unresolved recurrence (2026-09)

# ARC demonstration-driven rule inference

Use for ARC tasks where a test grid is accompanied by one or more demonstrations. Infer a transformation that generalizes, rather than matching a visual hunch.

## Procedure

1. **Parse the full instance.** Record dimensions, distinct colors, repeated backgrounds, exceptional shapes/markers, and any action/attempt/demo caps. Keep row/column coordinates explicit and use them consistently.
2. **Compare each demo cell-by-cell.** Align input and output at matching coordinates when dimensions match. List changed coordinates and their before/after colors; separately note additions, removals, recolorings, dimension changes, and preserved seed structures. If dimensions differ, identify segmentation or object-count mappings that explain the change.
3. **Form a small set of competing rules.** Consider geometry, relative position, orientation, counts, symmetry, lines/regions, and transparency. Do not infer an anchor, target color, or direction solely from visual resemblance.
4. **Replay candidates on the demo.** Apply each candidate to the full demo input and compare every output cell and dimension exactly. Reject rules that leave changes unexplained or predict changes in preserved cells. All demos should fit one rule, aside from supported parameter changes such as color or size.
5. **Use demonstrations economically.** A demo request has a cost. Request one only when a specific unresolved ambiguity could materially change the test output. First extract all constraints from existing examples and test concrete hypotheses; do not request merely because the rule is not immediately obvious.
6. **Apply the validated rule to the test.** Preserve unrelated cells unless demonstrations show otherwise. Verify bounds, row and column counts, allowed values, and output dimensions before submission.

# ARC task variant inference

Use when an ARC/Continual-ARC task identifier has appeared before, or when a familiar visual pattern may conceal a new generated variant. A task ID and remembered solution are clues only; the current demonstrations are authoritative.

## Workflow
1. **Start fresh from the current instance.** Parse its input and demos. Do not copy a prior answer or assume task-ID recurrence guarantees the same rule.
2. **Inventory candidate structures.** Mark background, isolated markers, compact prototypes, connected objects, and all non-background offsets. Use a consistent anchor, usually a marker cell or the prototype bounding-box origin, and state offsets explicitly.
3. **Compare demo input/output at identical coordinates.** Record changed and preserved cells, including colors. Distinguish which objects act as anchors from the motif being copied; infer transparency of prototype-background cells rather than assuming it.
4. **Test complete rules.** Reconstruct the entire demo output from each candidate. A valid rule must account for every changed cell and preserve all unchanged structure, not merely explain a visually salient portion.
5. **Use prior knowledge only as a candidate generator.** Where a task ID has known variants, retrieve the relevant note in `references/variant-examples.md`, then decide from the current demo which (if any) applies. Never transfer a motif, anchor, orientation, palette, or target-selection rule without evidence.
6. **Spend demos selectively.** Request another example only for a specific unresolved ambiguity whose answer could change the test output. Avoid reflexive requests when the demo already identifies a unique rule. With a limited action budget, weigh demo cost against the risk of a wrong submission.
7. **Apply conservatively to the test.** Preserve unrelated cells, bounds-check all copied offsets, and validate row/column counts, dimensions, and color range before submitting.
8. **Honor the interface exactly.** In Continual-ARC action-only sessions, output exactly one permitted action JSON object, with no prose, and include a grid only for submission.

## Confirmed denoising variant: task-16b1bf1f
Three demos establish an image-noise cleanup task. The grids contain a dominant background and coherent solid/rectangular color regions; scattered singleton or isolated foreign-color cells are noise. Restore each noise pixel to the underlying coherent region/background color, but preserve coherent objects even when they have uncommon colors. Examples: demo 1 (27x10, bg1) removed scattered colors 0/2/3/8/9 and restored cells inside color-6 forms to 6; demo 2 (13x28, bg5) removed singleton intrusions 1/6/9 in coherent color-4 and color-2 regions, retaining the region colors; demo 3 (12x26, bg5) removed isolated 2/3/4/6 artifacts while preserving coherent 7/8/9 structures. Test output was accepted after replacing all isolated speckle colors with underlying bg/object colors: test bg0, retain color1 and coherent color8 structures, restore isolated noise intrusions (including 7/5/2/9 within 8 forms and stray nonzero cells on bg) to the local structured color or bg. Four prior submissions were wrong; correct output also changed an anomalous notch within a coherent color-8 object (row 3 col 7 in the 0-indexed test) back to 8. Do not merely erase noise to background: first determine whether each speckle lies on an object or on background. Preserve connected/block-shaped objects such as the 1 regions and 8 forms.

A 29x26 demo had background 9, solid rectangular/connected objects in colors 2 and 5, and color-4 speckles. A verified general variant translates the entire non-background pattern down exactly one row: vacated top row becomes background, preserve colors and geometry, and clip anything shifted beyond the bottom. The 25x5 test (background 5, color-6 block with a 5 notch plus a separate color-6 singleton) was accepted with exactly this transformation. Thus the rule applies to sparse/simple shapes as well as more complex patterns. Treat recurrence as a candidate, and verify current demos when available.

## Confirmed separator-band replication variant: task-8e04f0ad
A demo showed a 29x5 grid with full-width separator rows of color 2 at rows 10 and 20 (1-indexed), splitting it into three 9x5 content bands. Output replicated that entire panel into all six panels, retaining separator lines (color 9). Its accepted 9x8 test had separators at row 4 and columns 2 and 5, yielding six equal 4x2 panels; the top-right source panel contained colored cells 4 and 3 in its final two rows, and the accepted output copied this pattern into each of the six panels while preserving separators (color 2). For this variant, identify the content panel/band with the non-background pattern and tile that complete region into all equal-sized regions partitioned by full separator lines. Preserve the separators and all colors/geometry. Demos may have multiple separators in one or both dimensions. Verify region dimensions and source-region selection; do not blindly infer from task ID if demos suggest another rule.

## Pitfalls
- **Task-ID anchoring:** a recurring task ID may have multiple generated variants. Never select a stored solution from the ID alone.

- **Incomplete audit:** verify both changed and unchanged cells, including the original prototype and border destinations.
- **Over-requesting:** an extra demo is not free. Ask only for a concrete discriminating case.
